models._description: Microsoft Service (AbstractModel: generic Microsoft OAuth2 + REST helper, no persisted fields)

behavioral_notes.element: microsoft.service._get_authorize_uri / _get_microsoft_tokens / _refresh_microsoft_token (generic OAuth2 authorization-code flow against login.microsoftonline.com)
behavioral_notes.observation: microsoft.service is an AbstractModel with no fields: it is a parameterized OAuth2 client shared by every Microsoft integration. _get_authorize_uri(from_url, service, scope, redirect_uri) builds the consent URL against the v2.0 authorize endpoint (microsoft_account.auth_endpoint ICP, default https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/v2.0/authorize) with response_type=code, access_type=offline (so Microsoft returns a refresh_token) and a JSON state carrying {'d': dbname, 's': service, 'f': from_url, 'u': database.uuid}. The client_id is read per service from the ir.config_parameter microsoft_<service>_client_id (treated as public, leakable in clear in the authorize URI), and the client_secret from microsoft_<service>_client_secret via the module-level _get_microsoft_client_secret(ICP_sudo, service) hook -- a deliberate indirection so the secret is only ever read inside a request and never returned to a caller in clear. _get_microsoft_tokens(authorize_code, service, redirect_uri) POSTs grant_type=authorization_code (with the default calendar scope 'offline_access openid Calendars.ReadWrite' from _get_calendar_scope) to the token endpoint (microsoft_account.token_endpoint ICP, default .../oauth2/v2.0/token) and returns (access_token, refresh_token, ttl); on requests.HTTPError it raises res.config.settings.get_config_warning. _refresh_microsoft_token(service, rtoken) POSTs grant_type=refresh_token to the same token endpoint and returns (access_token, expires_in). None of this token lifecycle is visible from field/model metadata.

behavioral_notes.element: microsoft.service._do_request (host-allow-listed outbound HTTP wrapper for all Microsoft API calls)
behavioral_notes.observation: _do_request(uri, params, headers, method='POST', preuri=DEFAULT_MICROSOFT_GRAPH_ENDPOINT, timeout=20) is the single choke-point through which token exchange/refresh and every downstream Microsoft Graph call make outbound HTTPS requests (via python-requests). It hard-asserts that the resolved host of preuri+uri is one of the hosts of DEFAULT_MICROSOFT_TOKEN_ENDPOINT (login.microsoftonline.com) or DEFAULT_MICROSOFT_GRAPH_ENDPOINT (graph.microsoft.com) -- a static SSRF/host allow-list. GET/DELETE pass params as query string; POST/PATCH/PUT send them as form data with the given headers. It returns a (status, response_json, ask_time) tuple where ask_time is parsed from the response Date header (used by callers for clock-skew-tolerant token-expiry math), maps the 204/404 RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND_STATUSES to an empty body, and swallows those statuses while re-raising every other HTTPError (logging the response content). This generic request/error behavior is pure code, absent from metadata.

behavioral_notes.element: /microsoft_account/authentication public controller (MicrosoftAuth.oauth2callback) -- shared OAuth2 redirect endpoint
behavioral_notes.observation: The single route (controllers/main.py, type=http auth=public) is the OAuth2 redirect_uri that Microsoft calls back after the user accepts/refuses consent. It JSON-decodes the round-tripped state param into {'s': service, 'f': url_return, ...} and raises werkzeug BadRequest if no service is present (or a code arrives without a return url). On success it reconstructs the redirect_uri from request.httprequest.url_root (falling back to user.get_base_url()), calls microsoft.service._get_microsoft_tokens(code, service, redirect_uri) to exchange the auth code, then hands the returned (access_token, refresh_token, ttl) to request.env.user._set_microsoft_auth_tokens(...) and redirects back to url_return. On an OAuth error it appends ?error=<reason> (or ?error=Unknown_error) to url_return. The module is thus a generic, service-agnostic token broker.

behavioral_notes.element: res.users._set_microsoft_auth_tokens convention + downstream consumption by microsoft_calendar / microsoft_outlook
behavioral_notes.observation: Unlike its google_account sibling (which persists nothing), microsoft_account itself defines the base token store: res.users is extended with microsoft_calendar_rtoken / microsoft_calendar_token (both groups='base.group_system') and microsoft_calendar_token_validity, and _set_microsoft_auth_tokens(access_token, refresh_token, ttl) writes those three fields, computing validity as now + timedelta(seconds=ttl). _set_microsoft_auth_tokens is the callback contract the controller invokes and the seam downstream modules override/extend: microsoft_calendar consumes microsoft.service for its calendar OAuth/refresh and reuses these res.users token fields and the /microsoft_account/authentication callback; microsoft_outlook reuses the same microsoft.service helpers and microsoft_<service>_client_id/client_secret ICP convention for SMTP/IMAP OAuth on mail servers. The per-service 'service' string is the parameter that lets one generic microsoft.service serve every integration with distinct client credentials and scopes. This callback/override convention is runtime behavior absent from metadata.

behavioral_notes.element: external integration -> Microsoft identity platform + Microsoft Graph (gap #7, static)
behavioral_notes.observation: Outbound HTTPS integration via python-requests to Microsoft, host allow-listed by assertion in microsoft.service._do_request to login.microsoftonline.com (v2.0 oauth2 authorize + token endpoints) and graph.microsoft.com (Microsoft Graph REST reached by downstream modules). The OAuth2 client_id (microsoft_<service>_client_id ICP, public, in clear) and client_secret (microsoft_<service>_client_secret ICP, never returned in clear, read only inside a request via the _get_microsoft_client_secret hook) are admin-supplied per Microsoft Azure app registration. The auth/token endpoints are overridable via the microsoft_account.auth_endpoint / microsoft_account.token_endpoint ICPs (sovereign/national clouds). A seed ICP microsoft_redirect_uri = urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob is shipped in data. No vendored SDK -- the OAuth2/REST client is hand-rolled in models/microsoft_service.py with a 20s timeout. This external SaaS dependency (Microsoft identity + Graph) is invisible to Python model/field metadata and is the defining trait of the module.

classification.rationale: microsoft_account is shared OAuth2/identity infrastructure: it owns no business object (an AbstractModel microsoft.service with zero persisted fields, plus three OAuth token fields grafted onto res.users; no security groups, no views) and produces no sellable output. It is the generic Microsoft OAuth2 + REST plumbing -- consent-URL building, authorization-code exchange, refresh-token renewal, a base per-user token store (_set_microsoft_auth_tokens) and a host-allow-listed outbound request wrapper -- on which microsoft_calendar and microsoft_outlook build by supplying a per-service 'service' string and microsoft_<service>_client_id/secret credentials. It is the direct sibling of google_account (same support/firm-infrastructure role). Per Stabell & Fjeldstad this is a support / firm-infrastructure function (activity_class=support). For APQC it maps to 8.0 Manage Information Technology -- specifically the external-system-integration / credential-lifecycle band: the module's entire reason to exist is third-party SaaS integration (gap #7: it talks to login.microsoftonline.com and graph.microsoft.com) and OAuth2 credential and token lifecycle management, which are IT-management concerns rather than business-capability development. This matches the 8.0 classification of google_account and of the downstream microsoft_calendar / google_calendar connectors. This is a deliberate departure from the inherited/baseline 13.0 'Develop and Manage Business Capabilities': 13.0 was considered but rejected because nothing here develops a new business capability -- it operates an external authentication interface and brokers tokens; 9.0 'Acquire, Construct, and Manage Assets' was also rejected since no physical/IT asset is managed, only API credentials and an OAuth2 token exchange.

standard_capabilities: generic Microsoft OAuth2 authorization-code flow reusable by any Microsoft service (calendar/outlook)
access_type=offline consent so Microsoft returns a long-lived refresh_token
authorization-code -> token exchange and refresh-token renewal against login.microsoftonline.com v2.0/token
single public OAuth2 redirect callback (/microsoft_account/authentication) that exchanges the code and stores tokens
base per-user token store on res.users + _set_microsoft_auth_tokens callback for downstream modules to extend
per-service client id/secret configuration via ir.config_parameter (microsoft_<service>_client_id / client_secret)
overridable auth/token endpoints for sovereign/national Microsoft clouds
host-allow-listed outbound HTTP wrapper (_do_request) for all Microsoft API traffic
typical_fits: downstream Microsoft modules (calendar, outlook) reusing one OAuth2 base instead of each re-implementing the flow
self-registered Microsoft Azure app registration: admin sets client id/secret per service in Settings
single shared res.users token store consumed and refreshed by the integrating module
common_gaps: token fields are calendar-named (microsoft_calendar_rtoken/token/token_validity) -- the base store is effectively single-credential, not cleanly per-service
no built-in UI: client id/secret config and any connect button live in base_setup / the downstream module
no automatic refresh scheduling -- _refresh_microsoft_token must be invoked lazily by the caller on expiry
no token-revocation endpoint call -- 'disconnect' is handled by the downstream module wiping the stored tokens
single-app credentials per service; no multi-tenant / per-company client credential isolation
_get_calendar_scope hard-defaults the token-exchange scope to Calendars.ReadWrite, biasing the generic base toward calendar

open_questions: Exact set of downstream 'service' strings in production (calendar / outlook / ...) and which still route their callback through /microsoft_account/authentication vs a module-local one.
Whether the calendar-named res.users token fields are reused as-is by microsoft_outlook or whether outlook keeps its own credential store on outgoing/incoming mail servers.

How clock skew is handled across services: ask_time is parsed from the Microsoft Date header in _do_request, but token-validity math (now + expires_in) lives in _set_microsoft_auth_tokens / each caller.
